classification.difficultyReason: The source supplies the diagonals, two variables and all intermediate targets. Match two same-chord angles, substitute in a triangle sum, then combine the split angle; a fully scaffolded theorem proof.

content.prompt:
Here is an alternative proof that: The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.

In the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, draw the diagonals AC and BD.

Let $\alpha=\angle DAC$ and $\beta=\angle BAC$.

spec.description: Cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, with A upper left, B upper right, C lower right and D lower left. Blue circle and quadrilateral sides; red dashed diagonals AC and BD. α lies between AD and AC at A; β lies between AC and AB at A.
spec.answerVisibility: All original givens/point identities retained, no computed student values or added proof segments.

answer.short: They stand on chords DC and BC respectively.
answer.worked: Angles DBC and DAC stand on the same chord DC, so $\angle DBC=\angle DAC=\alpha$. Angles BDC and BAC stand on chord BC, so $\angle BDC=\angle BAC=\beta$.

answer.short: Use the angle sum in triangle DBC.
answer.worked: In triangle DBC, $\angle DBC+\angle BDC+\angle DCB=180^\circ$. Substituting part a gives $\alpha+\beta+\angle DCB=180^\circ$, hence $\angle DCB=180^\circ-(\alpha+\beta)$.

Since AC divides the angle at A, $\angle DAB=\alpha+\beta$. Therefore $\angle DAB+\angle DCB=(\alpha+\beta)+180^\circ-(\alpha+\beta)=180^\circ$. This proves the opposite-angle result using same-arc angles and a triangle sum, without assuming the theorem being proved.
